articles.title: Metal Gear Solid 4: The Flawed Masterpiece Kojima Didn't Want to Make
articles.summary: With Metal Gear Solid 4 finally arriving on modern consoles thanks to Master Collection Vol. 2, we take a look back at the game's legacy. Was it really just a big cutscene, or is it Kojima's masterpiece?
body: This is an IGN opinion piece from Charlie Lopresto, who believes that love can bloom, even on a battlefield. He first encountered Metal Gear Solid on a demo disc from Pizza Hut and has since completed three hundred missions in VR– the kind that’s indistinguishable from the real thing.

Like Old Snake, Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots is a fossil. A genetic dead-end of gaming evolution, the unhinged and overflowing masterpiece that barely left a mark on the artform. Despite its commercial and critical success, MGS4 is rarely regarded as top tier Metal Gear. But is that actually fair?

Trapped on dead console hardware for the better part of its hard life, thanks to the new Master Collection Vol. 2 it’s finally possible for everyone to experience MGS4, from series diehards who first fired it up in 2008 to people completely new to Metal Gear who have absolutely no idea what they’re in for.

All of them will reckon with the many, many questions MGS4 brings to mind, like: Will we ever see a game like this again? Why did we stop talking about it? And, perhaps most importantly: MGS4 is really good, isn't it?
points: With Metal Gear Solid 4 finally arriving on modern consoles thanks to Master Collection Vol.
Was it really just a big cutscene, or is it Kojima's masterpiece?
He first encountered Metal Gear Solid on a demo disc from Pizza Hut and has since completed three hundred missions in VR– the kind that’s indistinguishable from the real thing.
Like Old Snake, Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots is a fossil.

articles.title: Ultra Graphics Settings Are a Scam: Why High Is Good Enough, if Not Better, for Most Players
articles.summary: Most games don’t actually need to be played at Ultra settings to look good. They don’t even need it to look great. To prove it, I turned down the settings in a bunch of great-looking games to see how much difference it really makes.
body: I’m a privileged gamer. As a hardware reviewer, over the years I’ve been sent top-tier CPUs and graphics cards, letting me bounce from one flagship to the next. That’s made me lazy at game settings. I often just set the game at whatever the maximum “Ultra” setting is and get on with playing. But by doing so, I’ve just been playing into the marketing hype – and leaving a lot of performance on the table, it turns out.

I’ve been able to ignore graphics settings for so long due to a mix of low-demand game selection and high-end hardware. As I said, my current system is powerful, but I also mostly play older sim games and lighter indies.

With an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D and PowerColor Red Devil RX 7900 XTX, I have one of the fastest gaming CPUs on the market and the fastest graphics card AMD has ever made. It’s not quite an RTX 5080 or RTX 5090, so it’s not really designed with Ultra Path Tracing in mind, but it’s not a million miles away either. It’s more than capable of running almost any game at Ultra settings, at 4K, and sometimes even with ray tracing enabled.
That’s especially true once you throw in FSR upscaling and a little frame generation to smooth things out.
points: Most games don’t actually need to be played at Ultra settings to look good.
To prove it, I turned down the settings in a bunch of great-looking games to see how much difference it really makes.
As a hardware reviewer, over the years I’ve been sent top-tier CPUs and graphics cards, letting me bounce from one flagship to the next.
I often just set the game at whatever the maximum “Ultra” setting is and get on with playing.

articles.title: Celebrate the SNES's 35th Birthday With the 5 Weirdest Switch Online Games
articles.summary: The Super Nintendo is 35 years old. The same as me. Rather than curling up and dying when I realized how much time has passed since 1991, I figured a better way to mark the occasion would be playing some SNES games.
body: I was five months old when the SNES launched in North America, an age hardly conducive to exploring the niche catalogue of a new console. I played Super Mario World and the video game versions of popular Disney movies, and then I moved on to PlayStation, Game Boy Advance, and so on. So when I opened the NSO app, I was surprised to find just how many unfamiliar-looking box covers were staring back at me and decided to check out as many as I reasonably had time for. Some hidden games deserve to stay that way forever (looking at you, Spanky's Quest ). But these five stuck with me and I'm glad I took the time for them.

articles.title: Sangster Directs Hammer Review
articles.summary: Sangster Directs Hammer review: Severin Films focuses on the considerable contribution of writer/director Jimmy Sangster (and actor Ralph Bates) to Hammer horror film history.
body: In a cute twist on Frankenstein tropes, Victor keeps track of creature assembly via a build-by-numbers approach. His friend Wilhelm (Graham James) even hits the nail on the flattop by speaking a version of the clichéd line: “You’re tampering with forces we don’t fully understand!” As for the creature itself, David Prowse (yes, Darth Vader) is a mute, hairless Karloffian monster with a creepy smugness that suggests he’s far smarter than his predecessors. He’s no tragic figure either; this creature’s a violent bastard. As the bodies mount up, Victor is willing to let those around him suffer if it means protecting his creation; the apple didn’t reanimate far from the tree.

The only disappointment is an abrupt ending that leaves you wanting Bates-led sequels, but it wasn’t to be; when Hammer tried one more time to draw on Shelley’s creation for movie material, they brought Cushing back. But we have this one, and it’s a twisted delight.

articles.title: Pokémon ETBs are Surprisingly Easy to Get Hold of Right Now on Amazon
articles.summary: Amazon has quietly restocked high-demand Pokémon TCG Elite Trainer Boxes below secondary market prices, including hard-to-find Pokémon Center Exclusives and new releases.
body: If you've been looking around the shelves over the last few months, then you've almost definitely realised that Elite Trainer Boxes (ETBs) are as hot as a Torkoal using Sunny Day at the moment, and they're flying off the shelves!

The intense popularity of the Mega Evolution expansion, the surge of nostalgia ahead of the franchise's 30th Anniversary, and the continuous pressure from secondary-market scalpers (thanks, Logan Paul ) have all contributed to the high demand for sealed ETBs. Will the retail frenzy ever end? One day, hopefully, but the realistic answer is most likely no, not for a while.

Yet, despite the odds, Amazon has quietly restocked a surprising range of high-profile ETBs at decent prices. I've tracked down the best deals I can find on Amazon US and UK right now; everything from the most recent summer releases to the hard-to-find Pokémon Center Exclusives to save you from your fights with the bots.

When you tally up the individual retail cost of buying nine standalone booster packs alongside official sleeves, dice, and custom storage, an ETB is pretty decent value. If you can get it at a decent price, that is. Fortunately, that’s where we come in!

body: Two graphics modes are planned across both consoles: a Quality Mode targeting 30fps at dynamic 4K, and a Balanced Mode targeting 40fps at dynamic 4K.
PS5 Pro will hit the same frame rates and resolution, but with what's being described as enhanced visual quality across both modes.

The absence of a 60fps option, even on higher-end hardware, has left some fans hoping for a post-launch performance patch, with others saying they'd have preferred a lower-resolution 60fps mode over a 4K cap at 40fps.

"60 fps on Pro? Cmon guys," commented one on YouTube. Another said: "It’s 2026, 60 fps is the bare minimum at this point". Some fans believe a 60fps patch has been confirmed, but we're struggling to find confirmation – we'll update if/when we hear more.

articles.title: Destiny 2's Slow, Painful Death Removes a Critical Third Space for Gamers
articles.summary: He stood on the roof of a decaying structure in the Plaguelands section of Old Russia on Earth while his girlfriend, Liv, stood a short distance away, perched atop a nearby building. Over their shared comms, Lord Saladin grimly recalled the fall of the Iron Lords. Across the way, Liv waved to Mac.
body: Across thousands of hours spent slaying gods and protecting humanity from the Darkness, one of the most important memories that Mac — better known as Mactics, a streamer and YouTuber who built a career helping hundreds of thousands of Destiny players master the game — has from the franchise seems like an unremarkable one.

“It’s quite random, but there was a sequence during the Rise of Iron campaign where the two of us were on opposite ends of a structure while some dialogue was playing, and she just waved at me and I waved back,” Mactics told Polygon via email. “This was after months of being apart, and I can’t remember a time since then that I had had a stronger feeling of being right by her side.”
Nearly a decade later, Mactics stumbled across that memory again while preparing to say goodbye to the game that helped keep them together.

articles.title: Amazon Is Under Fire After Leaking Jason Statham's New Movie
articles.summary: Is there anything better than watching an action-packed Jason Statham movie at the end of August? It's a great way to turn your brain off for a bit and unwind. On Aug. 21, action movie fans could hit the cinema to watch Mutiny, the latest addition to Statham's filmography.
body: As Deadline reported, Amazon accidentally leaked the entire Mutiny movie on Prime Video. Viewers who were curious clicked on it and were able to watch it before it was removed from the platform. Unfortunately for Lionsgate, the film's distributor, this gave internet pirates plenty of time to download it and share it on torrent websites.

In Mutiny, Statham plays the role of Cole Reed, a former soldier and cop who's retired to become a multimillionaire's personal bodyguard. He is wrongfully accused of a serious crime and follows the real perpetrators on board a cargo ship to seek revenge — the typical Jason Statham retired, ex-military arc that's always great fun.

Like Statham's The Beekeeper, Mutiny cost $40 million to produce. With low ratings from critics, its opening weekend was already shaping up to be shaky, and this ordeal may have made things worse. "They can now blame any box office underperformance on Amazon," said 007meow on a Reddit thread about the incident. User Bhu124 replied with "That's absolutely what they're going to do. No one is more happy this happened than Lionsgate. They're gonna get a f*ckton of money out of Amazon for this."
points: Is there anything better than watching an action-packed Jason Statham movie at the end of August?

articles.title: Silent Hill: Townfall's new gameplay trailer quietly confirms how long its PS5 exclusivity will last
articles.summary: A new Silent Hill: Townfall gameplay trailer has offered up over 18 minutes of first-look footage while also quietly confirming exactly how long the game's PlayStation 5 exclusivity will last.
body: The extended trailer follows protagonist Simon Ordell as he explores the fog-shrouded Shorefront region of the fictional Scottish island of St. Amelia, picking through houses and apartments, gathering items, and eventually running into some of the horrors lurking in the mist.

The trailer's closing fine print held the more notable reveal, though. Alongside reiterating that Townfall is a PS5 console exclusive, a caption confirmed: "Also available on PC. Not available on other consoles until at least 6 months after release date".
That's not a confirmed Xbox Series X/S or Nintendo Switch 2 release, of course, but it does give a rough window for when one could happen: from around March 2027 onward.

Developed by Screen Burn Interactive (the studio FKA No Code) and published by Konami and Annapurna Interactive, Townfall is also notable as the first mainline Silent Hill game to be played entirely in first-person. It's set to release on 24th September on PC and PS5.

articles.title: Fallout dev Tim Cain says we should pay more attention to bad games: '[Publishers] often don't learn from failure because they only look at the games that sold well'
articles.summary: "Jesus Christ, I could write this shit:" The great Alan Moore once said that the sort of negative inspiration you get from reading drivel is even more fruitful for aspiring authors than the kind you get from reading the classics.
body: Granted, he's not talking about irredeemable refuse like Leisure Suit Larry: Magna Cum Laude, but rather the "many" cases where "one game came out, it wasn't very good, and it was forgotten … you could learn a lot from games like that." You know, stuff like Viking: Battle for Asgard.

"For a publisher, their success is game sales. Because of that, they often don't learn from failure because they only look at the games that sold well," he said in the video. "Gamers will frequently point to popular games and say, 'we want more of that,' without necessarily knowing exactly what part of those games made them so good. If they do point to bad games, they tend to point to well-known bad games."

He likened the industry's tunnel vision on critical darlings, sales behemoths, and only the most prominent flops to survivorship bias. "In addition to looking for common features among games that sell well, you should look for common features among games that are considered unsuccessful."

articles.title: Double Fine confirms it owns all its games' IP and publishing rights after Xbox split
articles.summary: Double Fine has confirmed it owns – or will shortly own – the intellectual property and publishing rights to every game it made during its seven years under Xbox following the studio's split from Microsoft earlier this year.
body: CEO Tim Schafer confirmed the news on Kinda Funny Games (thanks, IGN ), fielding a fan question about whether buying Double Fine's back catalogue - including Psychonauts 2, Keeper, and Kiln - actually puts money in the studio's pocket.
"I saw a question there: 'Do you guys make the money on games?'" Schafer said. "The transfer of the IP came back to us, and we get the publishing rights back to all our games."
That said, "some of [the games]" remain with Xbox for the time being, but Schafer explained that "it just takes a while for it to all process".
"If you're curious, buying any of our games helps support the studio," he emphasised. "We can turn that money into revenue that helps us extend that runway."

body: There's so much - so much - invisible labour in making video games, but every now and then you catch something and it makes you think about the person who must have made that. One corner of your base in Star Wars: Zero Company has a little empty chair with an empty bottle next to it, facing out of one of its windows.It's not a pointed, deliberate discovery or anything, just the way the furniture in that area's been arranged. articles.title: This mod transforms Doom into a terrifying tactical shooter, and it's partly inspired by another PC gaming classic
articles.summary: It takes a brave soul to ask the question "What if Doom was an incredibly slow-moving tactical shooter?" In fact, it's not a question I ever thought I'd want an answer to—we aren't exactly short of grim-faced, hyper-lethal first-person shooters these days.
body: Blackout is a work-in-progress mod built for Doom source ports Zandronum and UZDoom, currently available in playable alpha. Created by modder PKmX, it's designed to provide "tactical military simulation-based gameplay that focuses on slow methodical clearing", according to a breakdown posted on the ZDoom forums, with players expected to "hide behind covers and execute proper breaching techniques to maximise chances of survival."

The mod makes several radical changes to Doom's basic playstyle. Movement is much slower, while your character is significantly more fragile. Weapons are based on real-life firearms that feature ADS and reloading, with damage and recoil that reflects their calibre, fire-rate, and so forth.

The enemies you face remain classic Doom monsters, but PKmX says their behaviours have been "tweaked to suit tactical gameplay". Attacks are deadlier but take longer to charge, and they can both suppress you and be suppressed by you. There's also a stealth and awareness system where gunfire draws monsters to your location, while remaining quiet may enable you to sneak past enemies unseen.
points: It takes a brave soul to ask the question "What if Doom was an incredibly slow-moving tactical shooter?
In fact, it's not a question I ever thought I'd want an answer to—we aren't exactly short of grim-faced, hyper-lethal first-person shooters these days.
